extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, law students, and legal practitioners interested in the theory and constitutionality of the administrative state
extracted.subtask_description: A short expository piece advancing a theoretical framework for evaluating the nature and constitutionality of administrative power, aimed at reshaping how rulemaking, enforcement, and adjudication are classified and judged. The piece presents the casebook's central concepts (nonexclusive vs exclusive power) and doctrinal implications (Chevron, rule categories, public vs private rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonexclusive power
rubrics_metrics.description: Much administrative power does not comprise unlawfully combined power, but rather this blended power, or what the casebook terms nonexclusive power. It terms such powers 'nonexclusive' because more than one branch can exercise them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: When President Washington issued regulations about payments and proofs for invalid veterans, he was enacting rules that Congress could have enacted but did not have to—hence nonexclusive legislative power. When agencies adjudicate public-rights cases, they are exercising a nonexclusive power that can, but need not be, exercised by the federal courts. The concept explains why many agency actions that appear to combine powers are instead single powers with multiple qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive (strict/pure) powers
rubrics_metrics.description: There are exclusive (or 'strictly' or 'purely') legislative, executive, and judicial powers that only the designated branch may exercise. Only Congress can exercise exclusively legislative power; some powers are exclusively executive or judicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of exclusive executive power include conducting war or prosecuting a case in court. Exclusive judicial power includes deciding cases under existing law affecting traditional private rights to life, liberty, and property; such matters must be adjudicated in courts under de novo standards of review. Delegating an exclusively legislative power violates the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blended/partaking qualities of governmental power
rubrics_metrics.description: Many governmental acts 'partake' of more than one type of power (legislative, executive, judicial), so activities like rulemaking, licensing, and adjudication can have mixed qualities rather than being pure instances of one branch's power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an agency promulgates a rule filling in statutory details with binding effect, it may be executing the law (executive) or exercising legislative power; when a license is issued under a 'public interest' standard, it has both legislative and executive characteristics; when the NLRB creates a new rule in retrospective adjudication, it may partake of all three qualities. Recognize these blended qualities rather than treating such exercises as unlawful combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutionality test based on exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The key constitutional inquiry is whether an agency is exercising exclusive power (impermissible if delegated improperly) or nonexclusive power (permissible when authorized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To the extent the administrative state exercises exclusive powers inconsistent with constitutional strictures for each type of power, it acts unconstitutionally. But much modern agency activity can be characterized as nonexclusive power and thus may be constitutional. This shifts the constitutional focus from 'combination' to 'exclusivity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of agency rules: legislative rules vs interpretative rules vs policy statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress must authorize agencies to promulgate 'legislative rules,' which are nonexclusive legislative power, whereas interpretative rules or policy statements are executive in character and do not require the same congressional authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nonexclusive/exclusive framework explains why the label 'quasi-legislative' and 'quasi-judicial' is appealing but ultimately misleading. Agencies should be permitted to make legislative rules when Congress authorizes filling in statutory details; interpretative rules and policy statements remain executive. This classification affects permissible delegation and procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-rights vs private-rights adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-rights cases can be assigned to courts or to the Executive (including agencies); when agencies adjudicate public-rights matters they are exercising nonexclusive power rather than the judicial power of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast, adjudication of traditional private rights (life, liberty, property) implicates exclusive judicial power and must be adjudicated in courts with de novo review. Whether an adjudication concerns public or private rights is therefore crucial to its constitutionality when performed by an agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinterpretation of Chevron deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Chevron cases do not involve agencies 'interpreting' law but rather agencies making policy—i.e., exercising nonexclusive legislative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the nonexclusive-power framework, Chevron deference is better understood as deference to agency policymaking authorized by Congress, not deference to judicially binding statutory interpretation. This reframes when and why deference is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological stance: serious formalism and originalism that allows administrative legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The approach takes formalism and originalism seriously but concludes that much, although not all, of the administrative state may be constitutional after all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological stance counsels rethinking traditional debates (which often echo 1930s controversies) by distinguishing exclusive from nonexclusive powers and recognizing that many modern administrative practices can be reconciled with constitutional structure under this framework.
